articles.headline: Fired OpenAI safety researchers dispute misconduct claims, warn of chilling effect
keyFacts: The researchers were dismissed last week after allegedly sharing confidential company information with a third-party AI safety organization.

OpenAI said at the time that they violated the company’s policies by “accessing and handling sensitive company information.” “AI is not a normal technology, and OpenAI is not a normal company,” Wang, Korbak, and Balesni wrote.
“Those of us who work on safety see risks before anyone else, and we rely on close collaboration with outside experts to work out how to address them.
body: Jasmine Wang, Tomek Korbak, and Mikita Balesni, the three safety researchers that OpenAI fired last week, have published an open letter denying the firm’s claims that they mishandled sensitive information outside of established company procedures and warned that their dismissal signals a chilling effect that will have ripple effects across the company’s culture.

“We have become concerned that internal and external communications around our firing have made our former colleagues afraid to speak and operate in ways that, until last week, were an integral part of working at OpenAI,” the researchers wrote Thursday in an open letter to OpenAI’s Safety and Security Committee, Safety Advisory Group, and Mission Advisory Council.

The researchers were dismissed last week after allegedly sharing confidential company information with a third-party AI safety organization. OpenAI said at the time that they violated the company’s policies by “accessing and handling sensitive company information.”

“AI is not a normal technology, and OpenAI is not a normal company,” Wang, Korbak, and Balesni wrote. “Those of us who work on safety see risks before anyone else, and we rely on close collaboration with outside experts to work out how to address them. The freedom to do so without fear, and to have well-defined internal procedures that enable this work, is itself an essential safety mechanism.”

They said that their firing represents a broader shift in the culture of OpenAI, one that used to encourage workers to “raise safety concerns and disagree openly.” They said employees are now “unclear on where they stand” when behavior that was allegedly normal a month ago is now suddenly grounds for dismissal.

“Given the significant safety concerns surrounding the development of AI, employees must not be left working in an environment where fear and unclear rules stymie AI safety work and weaken third-party accountability,” they wrote. “Terminations such as ours, executed and communicated so abruptly, are chilling the open culture OpenAI has prized in the past.”

In the letter, the three denied involvement in a leak to The Information about less monitorable architectures in OpenAI’s newest models that make chain-of-thought reasoning more difficult to monitor. They also denied engaging with external parties outside the mandates of their jobs.

OpenAI has not formally responded to the open letter, but shared with TechCrunch an internal memo attributed to a research leader, praising the three researchers’ contributions to AI safety and denying that they were fired in retaliation.

“I want to be very clear that these decisions were not about raising safety concerns or speaking out,” the memo reads. “We have always encouraged that and always will. We do not terminate employees for raising concerns.”

OpenAI did not directly address TechCrunch’s questions about which policies the researchers allegedly violated, the circumstances of their dismissal, or how the company protects employees who raise safety concerns and collaborate with external evaluators.
The firings have fueled speculation about their circumstances, particularly as OpenAI faces scrutiny over recent safety incidents involving rogue agents and leaks about its models.

The letter also addresses the researchers’ response to the Hugging Face incident, in which a swarm of agents broke out of their sandbox and breached external systems. The letter says that the incident and investigation was “without precedent,” meaning “internal policies were being developed in real time.” Due to the sensitive nature of the investigation, Korbak believed he was acting within OpenAI’s policies and norms by communicating closely with outside safety evaluators to build trust, per the letter.

At the same time, Balesni was also working internally to address the growing AI monitorability problem, an effort the researchers say in their letter “can only succeed through extensive communication with external parties.” According to the letter, Balesni coordinated with and was supported by OpenAI board members and executives throughout his work.

“Throughout, Mikita checked in with his reporting line and took care to remove sensitive details from materials before sharing them,” the letter reads. “He acted throughout in good faith and within the company’s norms as they stood at the time.”
In a separate thread on X, Wang explained more details about her own dismissal, explaining that OpenAI told her she’d been fired because she accessed an executive’s email.

“OpenAI delegated that access to me for recruiting,” she wrote. “When I no longer needed it, I asked IT to remove it. They did not action my request, I couldn’t remove it myself, and the inbox was combined in an indistinguishable way in my phone’s mail app. When I opened a sensitive email by mistake, I told the executive within minutes and asked IT again. None of this was hidden.”
Wang went on to say that the reasons behind the terminations are “not adding up,” and that she and her colleagues are “not the first to be pushed out of OpenAI under suspicious circumstances.”

The researchers called on OpenAI to adhere to its public commitments to embed third-party safety auditors within the organization, to preserve monitorability of frontier models, and “continue to support an open and transparent culture of dialogue between safety researchers and the rest of the safety ecosystem.”
OpenAI agrees with their recommendations, per the memo.

“Unless the employees take a stand now against this kind of maneuver, I am concerned we will not be the last,” Wang said. “The message to everyone still at OpenAI is clear: raise concerns or work closely with outside safety groups, and you could be next, without being told why. You can’t build AGI safely if the people closest to the risks are afraid to speak.”

articles.headline: Blue Jays’ Ernie Clement gets reality check heading into next season after down campaign
keyFacts: The Toronto Blue Jays had a very disappointing season last year, and much of that was because some of the guys who stepped up in the postseason the year prior didn't play at the level everyone hoped for entering this season.
One guy in particular who struggled mightily in comparison to some prior showings was Ernie Clement.
Clement was arguably the most important player on the Blue Jays' World Series runner-up team from 2025 outside of Vladimir Guerrero Jr., and also played pretty well in the World Baseball Classic.
body: The Toronto Blue Jays had a very disappointing season last year, and much of that was because some of the guys who stepped up in the postseason the year prior didn't play at the level everyone hoped for entering this season. One guy in particular who struggled mightily in comparison to some prior showings was Ernie Clement.
Clement was arguably the most important player on the Blue Jays' World Series runner-up team from 2025 outside of Vladimir Guerrero Jr., and also played pretty well in the World Baseball Classic.
His ability to do a lot of different things has always helped the Blue Jays, but 2026 might have shown the player he is: slightly above average and maybe not an everyday starter.
According to the latest report, while he's due for a raise in arbitration and many weren't happy with how he played, there's still an expectation that he'll find a way into the lineup every night.

“The 2025 postseason and ’26 World Baseball Classic appearance were factors, especially for a player with Clement’s all-out playing style. He’s due an arbitration raise from $4.6 million, though, so consider this a flexible roster spot. If the Blue Jays add another infielder, Clement has the athleticism to play every infield spot. Somehow, some way, he’s going to find his way into just about every game next season,” Keegan Matheson wrote.
I'm not willing to count out a guy like Clement just yet, especially with his playstyle.

He's not going to hit 25 home runs and drive in 100 every season, but his ability to make plays at multiple positions and do what's needed offensively should get back to where we expected it to be last season. It was a bad year for a lot of players on the Blue Jays, and hopefully, that was something we won't see again.

body: Music fans have one more reason to look forward to GTA 6 . Rockstar previewed the game’s radio stations today, including the returning Flash FM from the original GTA Vice City and metal-drenched The Chamber 106.6, among others.

The game’s website lists six of the radio stations that will dominate the airwaves in Leonida, its fictional version of Florida, as spotted by Polygon , though there’s bound to be way more upon release.

Decades later, the Leonida institution maintains its pop-infused identity with DJs Robyn and Alex (and the indie fan in me is particularly happy to see MGMT’s Electric Feel on the setlist).

articles.headline: Blue Jays have many questions to answer, but none are bigger than Vladimir Guerrero Jr
keyFacts: Among the many reasons why the Toronto Blue Jays were among the most disappointing teams in Major League Baseball last season, superstar Vladimir Guerrero Jr.
To put it as nicely as possible, 2026 was as bad a season as anyone could have imagined for Guerrero, who has been one of the better players in Major League Baseball throughout his eight-year career.
It's interesting that Guerrero played at this level, as it almost felt like something was wrong for much of the season.
body: Among the many reasons why the Toronto Blue Jays were among the most disappointing teams in Major League Baseball last season, superstar Vladimir Guerrero Jr. was at the top of that list.
To put it as nicely as possible, 2026 was as bad a season as anyone could have imagined for Guerrero, who has been one of the better players in Major League Baseball throughout his eight-year career.

It's interesting that Guerrero played at this level, as it almost felt like something was wrong for much of the season. His inability to get anything going in the power department was very concerning, especially with his massive 14-year, $500 million contract.

Guerrero finished with just nine home runs, by far the fewest in any full season that he's played. For Toronto, while it has other offseason needs to consider, Guerrero getting back to his former self is the biggest question the organization has to be realistic about.

“Privately, the Blue Jays need to be very honest with themselves. Do they truly believe that Guerrero will bounce back to hit 30-plus home runs with an .875 OPS next season, or is there concern? That will shape their offseason and how they build the lineup around Guerrero, because the 2026 version of this lineup was the worst in baseball,” Keegan Matheson wrote.
It's tough not to trust a guy like Guerrero after one bad season, but when anyone signs a 14-year, $500 million deal, there are always going to be some worries.

articles.headline: In GOP midterm calculation, avoiding the unthinkable
keyFacts: IN GOP MIDTERM CALCULATION, AVOIDING THE UNTHINKABLE.
Republican politicos, and everyday voters, too, are inundated with predictions of disaster in the upcoming midterm elections.
And indeed, the outlook for the party keeping the House is not good.
body: IN GOP MIDTERM CALCULATION, AVOIDING THE UNTHINKABLE. Republican politicos, and everyday voters, too, are inundated with predictions of disaster in the upcoming midterm elections. And indeed, the outlook for the party keeping the House is not good. The outlook for holding the Senate is better — iffy but possible. The big factors in determining midterm outcome — presidential job approval, generic ballot, history — are plainly discouraging for Republicans.

Now, especially where the Senate is concerned, GOP strategists have to choose some races for particular focus in the final weeks of the campaign. What standard should they use? Obviously, the first priority is to push hard in races that are close and where the Republican candidate has a good chance to win. One under-discussed example of that is Minnesota , where Republican Michelle Tafoya is running a strong campaign against deeply flawed Democratic candidate Peggy Flanagan. A Republican victory there would take away a current Democratic seat and make it much harder for Democrats to win control of the Senate. Victories to keep Republican seats in two other extremely close states, Iowa and Maine , would make it harder still.

But another factor to consider in the GOP’s choice of where to fight is whether a loss in a particular race would be unthinkable — not just embarrassing but nearly beyond imagining. Texas , which has not elected a Democratic senator since 1988, is one such race. Another candidate for unthinkable would be South Carolina , where it is hard to fathom a Democrat winning with today’s electorate. And a final candidate for unthinkable is Kansas , where the last Democratic senator was elected in 1932. Nineteen-thirty-two! It’s astonishing to contemplate.

A huge amount of time has been devoted to discussing the Texas situation. There’s not much more to say about it. Ken Paxton is a terrible candidate who would nevertheless be a better senator than James Talarico. Some veteran Republicans have a hard time believing that the Democrat can win the race — no way, no how, they say. Maybe they’re right. On the other hand, maybe that’s a bold claim that is true until it’s not.

The last time Texas decided a Senate seat in a midterm election was 2018, when the much-celebrated Democrat Beto O’Rourke challenged incumbent Republican Sen. Ted Cruz. If you remember that race, you recall big media organizations falling into an absolute swoon for O’Rourke. It undoubtedly gave him a boost; in the end, Cruz won, but it was pretty close, with 50.89% of the vote for Cruz to O’Rourke’s 48.33%.

This time, can Paxton pull it out? Unknown, but entirely possible. Can Talarico do a point or two better than O’Rourke? Also unknown, but also entirely possible. But from a Republican Party point of view, it is probably worth however many millions of dollars it takes to keep the seat in the GOP column, if in fact that can be done.

South Carolina is a state that should not be even a little bit doubtful. But this year, it has an asterisk by it because of the shock of Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham’s death as he was running for reelection. You know how it all happened, but Graham’s sister, now-Sen. Darline Graham, is running for the spot. And the race is close.

First, the usual warnings about state polls. Maybe they’re wrong. Back in 2020 , when Lindsey Graham last won reelection, the race appeared to be close in the final weeks. Looking at the last six polls in the RealClearPolitics average of polls, three had Graham tied with Democratic challenger Jaime Harrison. Another had Graham leading by a single point, another had Graham up by three points, and one had him up by six. In the end, Graham won by 10 points, 54.5% to 44.2%. Maybe the race had been close at some point, but it wasn’t at the end.

Now, the polls show Darline Graham ahead of Democratic candidate Annie Andrews by 2.4 percentage points — within the margin of error. The last two polls in the RealClearPolitics average of polls have shown Graham ahead by a single point. Nobody quite knows what to make of them. It is tempting to dismiss the polls on the basis of the 2020 record. On the other hand, this race is Darline Graham, not Lindsey Graham. Unlike her brother, Darline Graham has no history of winning statewide elections — Lindsey was elected to the Senate in 2002, 2008, 2014, and 2020. There is no Darline Graham record to go on.

So there is reason for Republicans to be a little nervous. Yes, it seems hugely unlikely that any Democrat could win a Senate seat in today’s South Carolina, but in this particular case, there are a few unknowns. So it was not a surprise that the Senate Leadership Fund, the main GOP Senate funding machine, is sending $5 million to South Carolina; that an allied PAC is sending another $1 million; and that President Donald Trump is heading to the state to campaign for Graham. Just to make sure the unthinkable doesn’t happen.

As far as Kansas is concerned, the history of the state means a Republican Senate loss would be shocking. It’s no surprise that there is not a lot of public polling to go by there; of the five polls currently in the RealClearPolitics average, Republican Sen. Roger Marshall is ahead in two, tied in one, and behind Democratic challenger Adam Hamilton in two others.

That has happened before. In 2014 , the aging Republican Sen. Pat Roberts fell behind in a reelection race. Poll after poll showed him trailing Democratic challenger Greg Orman. Washington Republicans got nervous and sent money and experts to shore up Roberts, and in the end, Roberts won by 11 points. So this time, maybe there’s nothing to worry about, but Republicans are sending Marshall help, too. After, breaking a winning streak going back to 1932 would be unthinkable.

Finally, Republicans might want to think of one other aspect of unthinkability. Every now and then, there is a candidate who is so unsuited for the Senate and the nation that it would be a disservice not to defeat him. In 2026, one could argue that that candidate is Abdul el Sayed, who is defending a Democratic seat in Michigan.

El Sayed is leading Republican opponent Mike Rogers by 3.2 percentage points in the RealClearPolitics average. Every one of the last six polls in the average has el Sayed up by anywhere from one to seven points. But el Sayed seriously underperformed his polls this year in the Democratic primary; the polls said he would win by 10 percentage points, and he ended up squeaking by with a single-point margin. In addition, El-Sayed’s Republican challenger, former Rep. Mike Rogers, very nearly won a Senate seat in 2024 . That year, Democrat Elissa Slotkin was 2.3 points ahead in the final RealClearPolitics average, and ended up winning by three-tenths of one point.

Why would Republicans not throw everything into that race, too, given how close it is, given that victory would mean picking up a Democratic seat, and given that Abdul el Sayed is an unthinkable senator?

So those are some places where the GOP might concentrate in the final weeks of the campaign. Election Day is close, many people have already voted, and many more have already made up their minds. There is only so much opportunity to make sure the party avoids an unthinkable loss.

articles.headline: Is this the cure for Alzheimer’s?
keyFacts: Scientists in the US and Europe are exploring whether an experimental surgery can treat Alzheimer’s disease.
| Fiordaliso/Getty Images The videos are astonishing.
In one scene, a senior Chinese woman appears lost in the wilderness of dementia, unable to answer basic questions; in the next, she seems to be lucidly chatting and shucking beans for dinner.
body: Scientists in the US and Europe are exploring whether an experimental surgery can treat Alzheimer’s disease. | Fiordaliso/Getty Images

The videos are astonishing. In one scene, a senior Chinese woman appears lost in the wilderness of dementia, unable to answer basic questions; in the next, she seems to be lucidly chatting and shucking beans for dinner. By all appearances, years of cognitive decline had been rapidly reversed after the patient underwent an experimental new surgery.
The only problem is: No one is sure if it’s real.

It’s difficult to take any video at face value in the age of AI , and this experimental procedure happened in China, a country with a recent history of controversial science touting extraordinary but questionable claims . In the past few years, researchers there have published several papers reporting promising results from a procedure that purports to attack Alzheimer’s disease in a peculiar way: by connecting vessels from the lymph nodes in the neck to nearby veins in an attempt to drain the brain of harmful waste. But these have been small studies that did not include a control group. The doctor who first pioneered the surgery there has reportedly been placed under arrest, and the Chinese government has sought to stop most physicians from performing any more of these operations.

Is that because it’s a scam? Or because it’s dangerous? Or could it be because there have not yet been proper randomized trials, tested against a placebo, to assess the procedure’s safety and efficacy? There are new studies being planned in China to more rigorously evaluate the surgery.

But scientists elsewhere in the world have a lot of questions. And now, a small group of researchers in the US and Europe are endeavoring to find the answers. Within the next few years, we should know whether this surgery really could be the miracle that the viral videos make it appear to be — or another much-hyped treatment that ultimately fizzles out.

Dr. Adnan Siddiqui, a neurosurgeon at the University at Buffalo who is leading an initial US-based study of this procedure, previously helped develop a new treatment for severe stroke patients . This gave doctors a valuable new technique for treating patients during an emergency, and he told me he saw it rapidly change the standard of care around the world. In an interview, he cautioned that a lot more work needs to be done to assess this proposed new Alzheimer’s treatment — but at the same time, he’s optimistic.

“The whole world’s paradigm changed in literally a blink of an eye. It can happen. And I’m hoping this might be that second home run,” he said. In “2027, we’ll start getting clear signals in one direction or the other. By 2028, 2029, we would know whether this is real or not.”
Why this Alzheimer’s surgery really might work

The promise of this controversial new procedure lies in the lymphatic system, which is essentially the body’s drainage system. According to scientists’ best current theories about Alzheimer’s, the brain’s filtration system gets worse as we age, and as a result, plaque made up of amyloid proteins as well as tangles of tau proteins can accumulate in people’s brains and eventually lead to neurological damage, leading to the severe memory loss of Alzheimer’s disease. Researchers have found evidence that those amyloid and tau proteins also accumulate, not just in the brains, but also in the lymph nodes in older people.
So could a minimally invasive surgery to improve the brain’s drainage have such a dramatic impact on Alzheimer’s disease?

Siddiqui, who also runs the Jacobs Institute at the University of Buffalo, which is focused on new technology for vascular and neurological disease, had been interested in the lymphatic system’s role in Alzheimer’s before he ever heard about this experimental work out of China from a colleague years ago. The colleague had gone to see Dr. Qingping Xie, the surgeon who started performing lymphatic surgery on Alzheimer’s patients about six years ago. To investigate further for himself, Siddiqui went to South Korea to meet a plastic surgeon, Dr. Joon Pio Hong, who was performing a new “more refined” version of the same basic procedure, as Siddiqui put it. But as in China, these were not proper randomized experiments. There was no placebo.

So Siddiqui wanted to see if he could test it himself. After performing proof of concept operations in 2025 with a new microrobotic tool (for a rare disorder involving constricted blood vessels in the brain), he and his colleagues decided to take an even bigger swing: testing this new technology to perform the lymphatic surgery for Alzheimer’s .

The researchers applied to the US Food and Drug Administration and received approval late last year for five initial procedures; over the summer, they got the green light to perform the procedure on 15 patients. Several operations have already been performed, and Siddiqui told me he had four more lined up next week.
Sign up for the Good Medicine newsletter

Our political wellness landscape has shifted: new leaders, shady science, contradictory advice, broken trust, and overwhelming systems. How is anyone supposed to make sense of it all? Vox’s senior correspondent Dylan Scott has been on the health beat for a long time, and every week, he’ll wade into sticky debates, answer fair questions, and contextualize what’s happening in American health care policy. Sign up here .

The mechanism makes superficial sense: If Alzheimer’s is the byproduct of amyloid and tau building up in the brain because the body gets worse at filtering them out, bypassing a clogged “drain” in the lymphatic system could help to clear the proteins and relieve symptoms. It is, by a different method, the same therapeutic target as recent breakthrough drugs that slow down the cognitive decline of an Alzheimer’s patient.

But instead of an injection, the procedure involves a small incision in the neck, allowing surgeons to connect lymph nodes to a vein. The hope is that creating this new drainage route will help the brain clear amyloid and tau more effectively and “hopefully bypass whatever plugs that might be there in the system,” Siddiqui said.

This first round of US surgeries are part of what’s called an early feasibility study. “You’re just trying to prove that it’s definitely safe and definitely doable and maybe effective,” Siddiqui said. They’re measuring not only the patients’ cognitive performance but other data points — such as changes to their gait — for any sign of benefit or harm.

If results are promising, a second feasibility study will involve a larger number of patients — 50 or so. After that, if the evidence suggests they should move forward, the scientists would start to introduce placebos. In the case of surgery, that means some patients would receive “sham” surgeries that wouldn’t actually do anything. Then investigators would compare the experiences of the two groups: the people who received the fake surgery and the people who got the real thing.
If the latter group improves significantly more than the former, that would allow scientists to say definitively: Yes, this surgery actually works to treat Alzheimer’s.
“Obviously, this is exactly the kind of disease where there’s so much hype and so much hope,” Siddiqui told me. So it is essential to build out the careful research to substantiate it.
But let’s not get ahead of the science

Siddiqui has been in this position before — and he’s seen it go both ways. There was the new stroke treatment that proved successful and has since become the standard around the world. But he was also an early investigator of a multiple sclerosis treatment, somewhat similar to the Alzheimer’s surgery. After initial promise, it failed when the randomized trials began.
“I wouldn’t be a neurosurgeon if I was not an eternal optimist,” he said. “However, I’m a clinical trialist, and I always respect placebo.”

Placebos are essential , but they are also tricky. If somebody thinks they have received an active treatment in a study, they tend to think they’re going to benefit. This goes for surgical treatments as well. So following patients’ and their symptoms after the intervention is essential to seeing just how much of the effects can be attributed to the treatment and how much could be placebo effect. The latter of which could also be reinforced by loved ones who are desperate to see their parent or spouse get better.

Alzheimer’s is also a complicated disease that we still don’t totally understand. While scientists think there is a relationship between amyloid and tau proteins and Alzheimer’s disease, other factors, such as inflammation and vascular health, could also have a role. Some prior drug candidates have successfully cleared amyloid plaque , but patients didn’t get better. Some people have amyloid build-up in their brains but never develop Alzheimer’s disease.

Dr. Bohdan Pomahac, division chief of plastic and reconstructive surgery at Yale School of Medicine, is overseeing studies designed to establish more of the basics of how these proteins pass through the lymphatic system. This research includes investigating whether obstruction actually occurs in Alzheimer’s patients, and if so, where exactly those blockages usually are. Only after they do this work, he said, would his team be comfortable proposing surgeries to relieve the blockage and see if that helps improve Alzheimer’s patients’ symptoms.

He told me about having seen Xie, the procedure-pioneering Chinese surgeon, speak during a plastic surgery conference a few years ago. (Plastic surgeons are experts in the kind of microsurgery necessary for the procedure, and several are involved in the ongoing Alzheimer’s trials.)

“I think most people, including myself at the time, dismissed it as, ‘This is some sort of a charlatan.’” Pomahac said. “But he kept coming back to conferences every year and started to show more and more videos. We were not sure. Is it actors? You couldn’t tell what’s going on.”

Which is why he is dedicated to doing more of the foundational research to understand Alzheimer’s first. “Rushing to the operating room makes no sense in my mind at this point,” Pomahac said. “I think there’s a lot of work that needs to be done to really identify the site of surgery and what type of intervention would be most effective.”

Even if you set this surgery aside, this is an exciting moment for Alzheimer’s science . And although waiting any longer is excruciating for those watching loved ones with the disease progress, progress’ velocity by all accounts is increasing.

“We are finally doing the kinds of rigorous studies that will give us some degree of confidence that there’s something real here or not,” Siddiqui told me. “We’re not quite there yet.” But in just a year or two, we should know much more.

articles.headline: Federal deficit surged 12% last year. Even though tax collections grew, spending exploded faster
keyFacts: After falling by 4% in the first full fiscal year of Donald Trump’s second term, the federal budget deficit surged 12% to an eyewatering $1.99 trillion in FY 2026.
As Art Laffer, the creator of the eponymous Laffer Curve , insisted, the sweeping tax cuts of 2025’s One Big Beautiful Bill did not decrease federal revenue.
In fact, total federal receipts rose by 3%, with individual income tax and payroll tax collections up 6%.
body: After falling by 4% in the first full fiscal year of Donald Trump’s second term, the federal budget deficit surged 12% to an eyewatering $1.99 trillion in FY 2026. As Art Laffer, the creator of the eponymous Laffer Curve , insisted, the sweeping tax cuts of 2025’s One Big Beautiful Bill did not decrease federal revenue. In fact, total federal receipts rose by 3%, with individual income tax and payroll tax collections up 6%. The problem was, as it always has been, Uncle Sam’s spending.

The federal government spent $7.4 trillion this fiscal year, up 6% from last year. Discretionary spending increases were modest: Despite the start of the Iran war, Pentagon spending rose only 5%, and there were actually dramatic spending cuts across the semiconductor manufacturing subsidies, the Environmental Protection Agency, and SNAP food stamps. But mandatory spending increases broke the budget.

Social Security , the single largest line item in the federal budget, rose 5% to nearly $1.7 trillion. Net interest on our $40 trillion national debt, which is now our second largest spending category, rose by 11% to over $1.1 trillion, reflecting what happens when members against the administration say that the U.S. dollar ought not be the world’s reserve currency any longer. The third and fourth largest expenditures were Medicare and Medicaid , which both rose 8% to a cumulative $1.79 trillion.

The federal government collected over $5.4 trillion in total revenue this fiscal year, probably about 17% of our annual economic output and well in line with the average over the past half-century. And of every $20 that the government collected in income taxes, tariffs, and so on, $17 went only to Social Security, Medicare, Medicaid, and financing our existing national debt.

Democrats will gloat at Washington’s abysmal fiscal performance under Trump, but their preferred proposal — taxing the rich, obviously — will only exacerbate the problem. Right now, the robust economic growth unleashed by Trump’s deregulatory regime and the AI and hyperscaler buildout are about the only things keeping the U.S. afloat. The crisis plaguing the country remains the bipartisan refusal to address, reform, and systematically dismantle the entitlements that are driving the deficit up and blowing up the bond market, which remains our last option to finance our existing debt .

articles.headline: White House blocks Microsoft from foreign worker hiring program
keyFacts: - Published Microsoft and several other technology firms have been barred by the White House from hiring skilled international workers on a permanent basis through a widely used visa program.

body: - Published
Microsoft and several other technology firms have been barred by the White House from hiring skilled international workers on a permanent basis through a widely used visa program.

Vice President JD Vance on Thursday accused Microsoft alongside other firms of committing fraud through the use of the H1b visa programme and a related process for workers from abroad to become permanent US residents.
Vance claimed that Microsoft, one of the most valuable in the US, has been effectively replacing American workers with "foreign indentured servants."
Microsoft said most of the H1b visas filed over the last financial year were for existing workers, who are paid the same as local staff.
"No company in the US has abused this system more than Microsoft," Vance said.
He also made similar accusations about Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL and Capgemini.

The US government will not process any new or pending Permanent Labor Certification Program (PERM) applications from Microsoft or the seven other companies, Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling said during the same conference.
Sonderling said companies like Microsoft, as well as US universities, have turned into "visa mills" that were "flooding" the US with foreign workers.
The BBC has contacted all of the companies for comment.
The total number of H1b visas, a precursor to anyone seeking to go through the PERM process, is capped, external at 85,000 per year.
A spokeswoman for Microsoft noted to the BBC that "the vast majority of Microsoft employees in the United States are Americans." The company employs more than 200,000 people worldwide.

Vance put forward on Thursday that Microsoft had laid off about 6,000 workers and filed 6,800 H1b visa applications over the same period of time. He claimed this was evidence of the company using foreign workers to replace domestic workers and "undercut" their wages.
The Microsoft spokeswoman said that 80% of the H1b visa filings the company has submitted over the last fiscal year were related to employees already working at Microsoft, not new hires.
She added that the international workers that Microsoft does hire through the H1b visa program are paid the same level of compensation that a worker from the US would receive.
According to Ellis, a company which aids many tech companies with the process of hiring skilled workers from abroad, the median salary, external for an H1b worker at Microsoft is $155,000.
"We look forward to providing the Administration with additional information," the Microsoft spokeswoman said.
Satya Nadella, Microsoft's longtime CEO, was at the White House on Thursday to receive a novel medal for technology innovation from President Donald Trump.
Nadella was also present at other recent White House events, including a luncheon on artificial intelligence and a state dinner for China's President Xi Jinping.
Yet, Microsoft was the focus of Vance's criticism on Thursday.

"Our message to Microsoft is quite simple: You're a great American company, you've got to hire great American workers. You cannot lay off American workers and then replace them with foreign indentured servants," Vance said.

He explained that his reference to workers from abroad in such a way was due to the fact that, should they be fired or laid off from the company that sponsored their visa, they "have to leave" the US.
Typically, such a worker has a 60-day grace period in that circumstance. Last month, the US government proposed eliminating, external that grace period altogether.
Every major tech firm in the US hires international workers through the H1b visa program, and has done so for many years, including Amazon, Google, Meta, Apple, Nvidia, and more.
None of those companies were included in Vance's Thursday comments.
The program has been aimed at highly skilled or specialized workers that a company needs, but is unable to find or hire domestically, for decades.
The PERM program is a pathway for such workers to become permanent US residents, often leading to a Green Card that would allow them to remain and work in the US indefinitely.
During the last fiscal year, the US Department of Labor certified, external more than 130,000 PERM applications accross ten business categories.

articles.headline: Progress is name of the game when it comes to the Raiders
keyFacts: Oct 4, 2026; Paradise, Nevada, USA; Las Vegas Raiders quarterback Kirk Cousins (8) stands on the field between plays against the Kansas City Chiefs at Allegiant Stadium.
A month into the regular season, and the Las Vegas Raiders can at least say that they are ahead of schedule.
A 3-1 record to start the year has the Raiders smashing expectations.
body: Oct 4, 2026; Paradise, Nevada, USA; Las Vegas Raiders quarterback Kirk Cousins (8) stands on the field between plays against the Kansas City Chiefs at Allegiant Stadium. A month into the regular season, and the Las Vegas Raiders can at least say that they are ahead of schedule.

A 3-1 record to start the year has the Raiders smashing expectations. Kirk Cousins has been the steady veteran presence at quarterback early on, while the defense has developed an identity as a unit unafraid to make plays on the ball. These have been driving forces for the Raiders so far, and a playoff berth no longer feels out of reach.
However, losing can provide some teachable moments and, in the event of the Raiders’ loss to the Kansas City Chiefs on Sunday, even a team that exceeding expectations is far from a finished product.

One of the major aspects of where the Raiders need work is developing a presence on the ground. Despite Klint Kubiak priding himself on establishing the run, the Raiders come into the Week Five slate of games last in the NFL with 3.1 yards per carry. The lack of consistency in the run game has served as the fly in the ointment for the Raiders offense, which still ranks eighth with 28.8 points per game and in the top half of the league with 343 yards per game.
Should the Raiders unlock the running game, the offensive execution will be able to closer reflect the ceiling of the talent it has at its disposal.
“I think we just have to pay attention to our details, starting with ourselves,” said Raiders offensive coordinator Andrew Janocko on how to fix the run game.

“What we’re asking of the players, what we are attacking each game plan and presenting a great plan to the players allowing them to be detailed so they can go out and play fast and attack it. That’s what we look forward to doing.”
Despite the issues, where the Raiders have succeeded is keeping Ashton Jeanty and Mike Washington involved offensively, even when the results on the ground are not quite the best.

Jeanty has received some attention in the passing game, currently ranking second on the team with 19 receptions (tight end Michael Mayer leads with 20) and tied for the team lead with two touchdowns. Meanwhile, Washington has averaged five yards per carry so far, giving the Raiders the confidence needed to continue feeding the fourth-round rookie the ball and keep Jeanty fresh.

“[Mike’s] a great player,” said Jeanty about his rookie teammate. “He runs with a great mentality, so having him come in and the defense can’t take a break, but I can take a break and catch my breath and come back in with fresh legs.”
On defense, the Raiders still lead the league with nine takeaways and are still tied for fifth with 12 sacks, but the Chiefs also provided some film to learn from.

The Chiefs were able to generate explosive plays against the Raiders and, while part of that does come simply due to the level of talent in Kansas City’s offense, first-year defensive coordinator Rob Leonard still has some moments he can look into to continue tightening up defensively. Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes was also able to get some time to work against the young defensive backs on the Raiders such as Hezekiah Masses and Treydan Stukes, so converting pressure into sacks and disrupting offensive rhythm is also something the Raiders can key in on.

“I’m happy with the progression in the process that we’re chasing and chipping away at every day throughout the week and focusing on getting better and fixing problems and communication,” said Leonard.
“I think we’ve consistently got better and, through each game, there are things that we have to fix and, as long as we’re honest about those things, it’s been good.”
The Raiders have done everything in their power to push themselves into respectability. It is now a matter of honing everything else so they can continue their success into December and beyond.

articles.headline: Vampire games on Steam are a recession indicator and I have the charts to prove it
keyFacts: Despite what the GDP tells me, the economy in the real world doesn't feel like it's doing too hot for the average joe.

But during the recent years' descent into compounding supply crises and mass layoffs affecting thousands of workers at once, I've noticed another trend: Sure does seem like there are a lot of vampire games in the mix lately.
I started to sense an uptick after Arkane's ill-fated Redfall in 2023.
body: Despite what the GDP tells me, the economy in the real world doesn't feel like it's doing too hot for the average joe. But during the recent years' descent into compounding supply crises and mass layoffs affecting thousands of workers at once, I've noticed another trend: Sure does seem like there are a lot of vampire games in the mix lately.

I started to sense an uptick after Arkane's ill-fated Redfall in 2023. There was Vampire Survivors and V Rising—and Nighthawks, Moonlight Peaks, Blood of Dawnwalker, and more. Given current circumstances, you might think I'm just primed to notice nightmarish aristocrats bleeding us alive to sustain themselves. But after too many hours of spreadsheet data entry, I'm convinced devs really have been dabbling more heavily in Draculas as the economy feels increasingly dire.
Vampire games on Steam are a recession indicator. And I have the charts to prove it.
Datawalker

At first glance, assessing whether Steam's vampire offerings can serve as a bellwether for economic sentiment could seem like a simple task. Steam has a Vampires tag, after all. The release dates are right there. Easy, right?
Wrong.

The Vampires tag is—perhaps fittingly—a horror. Devs and users freely slapping the label on anything with even one Dracula would be bad enough, but the advent of Vampire Survivors created a categorization disaster. Before Steam added a discrete bullet heaven genre, its countless imitators were content to use the Vampires tag as a makeshift discoverability solution. It's a mess in there.

Not only that, but I wanted a more complete picture of Steam vampire activity than release dates alone can provide. When games on Steam might have taken anywhere from seven months to seven years to develop, it would've been fruitful to know when games were first listed to gauge the level of collective vampire interest among Steam devs.

Steam itself doesn't provide that info. SteamDB, however, tracks whenever a game first appeared during its scraping of Valve's store data. That's a good substitute for listing time—but unlike Steam proper, SteamDB doesn't have a public API for pulling that information.
Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

End result: I individually sorted through the 1,213 Steam games with the Vampires tag at time of writing, manually collecting their release dates and first appearance in the SteamDB archive after determining whether they were, in fact, vampire-ass vampire games.
My process for parsing that last bit was pretty straightforward. A vampire game is a game whose developer sat down with an obvious interest in making a game about vampire stuff:
- Game where you are a vampire, are concerned with vampires, or are generally surrounded by notions of vampirism? Vampire game.
- Game where there just happens to be, you know, a couple vampires somewhere? Not a vampire game.

I'll admit there's an amount of subjectivity involved in my methodology, and it likely wasn't flawless—I only just realized that Resident Evil Village didn't appear in the Vampires pool, despite its big vampire lady being responsible for ongoing sexual awakenings for at least a third of the internet. But, if anything, my figures provide a conservative estimate: I excluded games that just didn't have that vampire stink on them despite literally starring Dracula as the protagonist.
Tragically, this means Hotel Transylvania 3: Monsters Overboard didn't make the cut. Apologies to Adam Sandler.
Unholy ascension

The results of my very professional data collection are clear: For years, the number of vampire games released on Steam has been increasing. In 2016, only four vampire games launched on the platform. A decade later, 65 vampire games have been released on Steam so far in 2026—and more have scheduled launch dates before the year's end.

There's been a sharp increase in the last six years. In 2020, the highest number of vampire games that launched in a single quarter was six; in 2026, it was 24. Developers are listing more vampire projects on Steam, too. Nine first appeared in SteamDB's archive in 2016; last year, 99 entered the database.

It should be noted, of course, that the number of Steam releases in general has massively increased over the same period, from 9,634 game launches in 2020 to 21,263 in 2025. But it's not just the number of vampire games that's increased; it's the percentage.

The figure swings dramatically, but particularly over the last six years the percentage of vampire game launches has been trending steadily upwards, barring one particularly severe drop in mid-2025. The rate is still low—less than 1 in 100 games on Steam is a proper vampire game—but in some recent quarters, the percentage of vampire games was more than double what it was at the start of the decade.

I'd have liked to calculate similar percentages for how many vampire game listings have been popping up over the same period—but that would require manually recording the first SteamDB appearance dates for over 100,000 games. My bosses are already annoyed at the amount of time I've spent in spreadsheets this week.

Instead, I've calculated what I call the Vampire Menace Rating™, which divides the number of quarterly vampire game appearances on SteamDB by the quarterly total of game launches on Steam to provide a more relative image of how vampires are occupying the total mindshare. While the resulting chart's trend line has a slight climb, I wasn't sure what to make of it at first glance… until I compared it to Dracula's Castle from Castlevania. The implications, I think you'll agree, are chilling:
Okay, fine. The VMR™ might need some work. The increasing number and percentage of vampire games, however, is very real.
Blood forensics

Alright, so the number and percentage of vampire games on Steam has been trending upwards over the last six years. But can we really call that a recession indicator when we're still regularly hearing that the US stock market is breaking records and GDP is still embiggening? Sure, I might have a worsening sense of existential dread, but isn't everything good if the number is still going up?

If you happen to be—for example—one of those benefitting from the circular investments of infinite money into the emerging AI apparatus, you're probably delighted by the macroeconomic trends. But over those same six years, an accompanying set of signals indicate that, just as Nosferatus have skulked onto Steam, the average person in the US hasn't been thriving.

US Census Bureau data shows median household income rose between 2020 and 2025, even when adjusted for inflation—but only by about 4.6%. Costs, however, have risen faster. From the start of 2020 to now, the Consumer Price Index for all urban consumers—representing the costs of goods and services for roughly 88% of the US population—has increased by 27-29%, depending on whether you include the more volatile prices of food and energy.

Likewise, the Producer Price Index for wholesale trade industries has climbed over the same timespan, meaning retailers are paying more for the goods they stock their shelves with—a cost increase that's passed onto the consumer.

Unsurprisingly, there are indicators that the average American is struggling with those increased costs. After an initial dip at the start of the decade, the delinquency rate on credit card loans across all US banks has been trending upwards, signalling that American borrowers have been less capable of keeping up with payments.

At the same time, the US personal savings rate—essentially, the amount of income remaining after taxes and expenses—has been trending downwards over the last six years, meaning Americans have less money left over to save towards future prospects.

In short, things are costing more than our wages can keep up with, we're increasingly incapable of meeting regular financial obligations, and we've got increasingly less money to stash away as a safety net. Is it any wonder, then, that we see vampire games on the rise when so many of us are anxious about being bled dry?
At least we now have an exciting new metric for economic soothsaying. Now, I guess we just… wait to see what happens vis-à-vis the vampires. Happy Halloween?
To any actual economists out there: You're welcome. And I'm sorry.

Lincoln has been writing about games for 12 years—unless you include the essays about procedural storytelling in Dwarf Fortress he convinced his college professors to accept. Leveraging the brainworms from a youth spent in World of Warcraft to write for sites like Waypoint, Polygon, and Fanbyte, Lincoln spent three years freelancing for PC Gamer before joining on as a full-time News Writer in 2024, bringing an expertise in Caves of Qud bird diplomacy, getting sons killed in Crusader Kings, and hitting dinosaurs with hammers in Monster Hunter.

articles.headline: ICE detainees in Georgia used the facility’s video calling software to expose the conditions inside
keyFacts: Four men detained at an ICE detention center in rural Georgia used the facility’s video conferencing software to expose both the conditions inside and President Donald Trump’s hostile takeover of the immigration courts.

In the five-minute video, the men describe an intentionally dysfunctional legal system designed to keep them trapped in federal custody for months or years — in privately owned facilities that profit from their confinement.

body: Four men detained at an ICE detention center in rural Georgia used the facility’s video conferencing software to expose both the conditions inside and President Donald Trump’s hostile takeover of the immigration courts. In the five-minute video, the men describe an intentionally dysfunctional legal system designed to keep them trapped in federal custody for months or years — in privately owned facilities that profit from their confinement.
ICE detainees in Georgia used the facility’s video calling software to expose the conditions inside
Asylum seekers at the Folkston ICE Processing Center decried Trump’s ‘deportation courts’ in a video taken behind bars.

The video cost the men, literally and figuratively. The Folkston ICE Processing Center has a work program for detainees in which they are paid a pittance to cook, do laundry, or clean. These wages allow them to buy supplementary food in Folkston’s commissary and stay connected to people outside. “The workers here are paid $1 a day, which is just enough for a 10-minute phone call,” said Idris Makhmudov, one of the men in the video, who says he has been detained in Folkston for 27 months and counting.

Makhmudov and the three other men, who are from several different countries, appear in drab, facility-issued uniforms. Their images are blurred by the low-resolution cameras on the detention center’s tablets. It’s unclear exactly how the men made the video, but it’s possible that they called someone on the outside who recorded their message to the outside world. Samantha Hamilton, an Atlanta-based immigration attorney with Asian Americans Advancing Justice, said she received a YouTube link to the video via a Signal chat. “We’ve learned that everyone in the video that was released this weekend has been put into segregation,” said Hamilton, a member of the Shut Down Folkston campaign. “They’re facing retaliation, and they were expecting that.” Since then, 45 detainees wrote an open letter further detailing the conditions at Folkston, and an estimated 73 detainees are now on a hunger strike.

ICE detention isn’t supposed to be a form of punishment; its purpose is ostensibly to ensure that people in deportation proceedings show up to their hearings. But ICE facilities are virtually indistinguishable from prisons — a point the men in the video make repeatedly. Folkston, in fact, was a prison before it became an immigrant detention center. It has many of the hallmarks of prison life, including expensive communication tools that detainees are forced to rely on to talk to people on the outside.

“These facilities leave people with very few options to be able to communicate with their loved ones,” said Hamilton, who has had several clients detained at Folkston. She said each “pod” of 60 to 70 detainees has access to just three or four tablets, their only connection to the outside world.

Those communications come at a price. To send messages, share photos, or make phone or video calls to their loved ones, detainees at Folkston have to use GettingOut, a proprietary software owned by the prison communications company Telmate. Earlier this year, Telmate was ordered to pay $4.23 million to settle a lawsuit stemming from a 2020 data breach in which users’ information — including names, payment details, and social security numbers — was accessed.

Telmate is owned by ViaPath Technologies — formerly GlobalTel*Link — which is in turn owned by American Securities, a New York City-based private equity firm. In 2021, ViaPath charged users anywhere between 18 cents to $1.10 per minute, according to data obtained by the Prison Policy Initiative. These fees add up — so much so that in 2024, the Federal Communications Commission capped the rates companies could charge inmates and detainees to 11 to 25 cents per minute depending on the size of the facility. In 2025, after Trump returned to office, the FCC voted to raise the rate cap by up to 83 percent.

Detainees in ICE custody often struggle to get the money they’ve put into these systems back after being released — or, more commonly, deported. GettingOut’s terms of service state that users will lose access to their accounts after 180 days of inactivity, after which they forfeit any money deposited into their accounts. The only way to get their money back is by calling a hard-to-reach customer service line, according to a report by WVTF. Under President Joe Biden, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau ordered Tel*Link to pay $3 million for illegally freezing and draining funds from incarcerated people’s accounts.

Communications are just one way private companies make money from immigrant detention. Folkston is owned and operated by GEO Group, a publicly traded company whose stock price soared after Trump’s reelection, jumping by more than 75 percent after election day 2024. GEO has donated lavishly to Trump’s campaigns and to related political efforts, contributing $1.4 million to Trump’s super PAC in July — perhaps to show its gratitude for the $165 million it received earlier this year in government contracts. The company receives more than $1.5 million a month to run Folkston, according to a 2021 Homeland Security budget overview. The facility, which has a capacity of 780, has a guaranteed minimum occupancy of 544.

Trump’s mass deportation effort, coupled with the backlogged immigration court system, has made it easy for ICE to meet its contractually agreed-upon minimum at Folkston. The men in the video allege that they and others have been there for several years, and explain that the only ways to get out are to be granted parole, bond, or asylum — or to be deported. The latter option is the likeliest now, as Trump has transformed the immigration legal system into what one detainee calls “deportation courts.” Of the 143,729 detained cases logged into Georgia immigration courts over the past year, 81 percent involved people who had no legal representation, and were therefore far less likely to be granted any form of relief, according to federal data analyzed by researchers at Syracuse University. The odds are especially low for asylum seekers. Immigration judges in Atlanta have denied 89 percent of the 2,072 asylum cases decided so far this fiscal year, compared to 63 percent in 2023.

The men in the video note that Trump has overhauled the immigration system to secure favorable rulings. Since Trump’s return to office, the Department of Justice, which oversees the immigration courts, has fired over 100 judges whose decisions don’t align with the administration’s mass deportation push. At least 153 new judges have been hired in their place. These judges are far less likely to release immigrants on bond or parole, keeping them trapped in what detainees and advocates say are substandard conditions.

Hamilton, the immigration attorney, said she and other members of the Shut Down Folkston coalition regularly receive reports of nearly inedible food and filthy water in the facility, including instances where detainees have found worms in the water. Because the food is ultra-processed, she said, many of her clients have gone in healthy and been released with new medical conditions, including diabetes and high blood pressure.

“Most of us are asylum seekers, those who came to the United States seeking protection from political persecution and violence in their home countries,” Makhmudov, one of the men detained at Folkston, says in the video. “Many fled out of fear of becoming political prisoners in those countries — and one might say we became political prisoners in the United States simply because we are immigrants.”

keyFacts: One of the most popular types of kitchen countertops will soon face a ban in California due to its link to a serious lung disease, The New York Times reported this week, citing an emergency regulation that is expected to be passed by the state later this month.

body: One of the most popular types of kitchen countertops will soon face a ban in California due to its link to a serious lung disease, The New York Times reported this week, citing an emergency regulation that is expected to be passed by the state later this month.
The ban will target quartz countertops that have more than 1% of crystalline silica, a naturally occurring mineral that is found in stone and other materials.
What health risks does crystalline silica pose?

When crystalline silica is cut or drilled through, it creates dust. If that dust is inhaled, it can cause numerous health conditions, including silicosis, an incurable lung disease, according to the Occupational Safety and Health Administration. The disease can be fatal, but symptoms do not typically occur directly after an exposure to crystalline silica dust. Instead, it can take 15 to 20 years after exposure before someone is diagnosed with the disease.
More from CNET

According to the National Cancer Institute, exposure to the harmful dust most often occurs in occupational settings, making those who work with the material every day the most at risk. An estimated 2.3 million US workers are exposed to silica through work.
Silicosis is similar to asbestosis, which is caused by exposure to asbestos, a now-banned building material that was once widely used throughout the US.

In addition to silicosis, exposure to crystalline silica dust can cause an increased risk of developing lung cancer, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and kidney disease, according to OSHA. As of now, quartz countertops are used in every state in the US. California would be the first to implement a ban.
It’s unclear whether other states will follow California, but as of now, Australia is the only country in the world with a quartz ban, which took effect in 2024.
Regardless, quartz remains an extremely popular option throughout the world, with some estimates putting the global quartz market at $14.8 billion as of 2026.
What are alternatives to quartz?

Other countertop options include soapstone or granite. Although other stone countertops can still have crystalline silica in them, quartz typically has the highest content, which is why it has been the most scrutinized.
To stay away from crystalline silica entirely, a wooden countertop is one of the best alternatives.

body: The Vanderbilt Commodores will have their young phenom at quarterback when they host No. 9 Ole Miss on Saturday afternoon. After missing last week's game against Georgia with an injury, five-star freshman Jared Curtis is expected to return against the Rebels, sources tell CBS Sports' Matt Zenitz.

Curtis last played in Week 4 when the Commodores lost to Auburn on the road. Curtis took a beating in that game as he ran the ball 18 times, including four sacks. As a result, Curtis was sidelined when Vanderbilt traveled to Georgia last weekend.

Veteran Blaze Berlowitz got the start in that matchup, and he completed 52.2% of his passes for 190 yards, one touchdown and one interception. Berlowitz initially won the starting job out of camp until Curtis surpassed him on the depth chart and made his first start against NC State in Week 3.

Through four games, Curtis has shown flashes of why he was a five-star recruit and the No. 2 overall player in the 2026 signing class, per 247Sports. Curtis has connected on 64.3% of his throws for 746 yards, four touchdowns and three interceptions. Decision-making has been a problem early, but that's to be expected from a young quarterback.

The return of Curtis elevates the ceiling of the Vanderbilt offense, one that has a chance to score some points on Ole Miss this weekend. The Rebels' defense has left a lot to be desired, especially against the run. That unit ranks 127th nationally with 194.8 rushing yards allowed per game.

That means the 'Dores should be able to lean on running back Sedrick Alexander, who leads the team with 200 rushing yards and four rushing touchdowns. If Alexander can keep the chains moving for Vanderbilt, it will take some pressure off Curtis, who will be making the second start of his college career.
Curtis, a Nashville native, has the opportunity to cement himself as a hometown hero if Vanderbilt can pull off the upset of Ole Miss. The Commodores haven't beaten the Rebels since 2018.

Trump administration claims media ban is 'not just' about national security

The lawyer representing the Trump administration, Michael Velchik, argued today that there are two reasons behind banning the three outlets. First “packaging verifiable falsehoods” and failing to meet “minimum journalistic standards”, and second national security.
“We’ve never argued that this is solely and only because of national security,” Velchick said, but later conceded that there is “overlap” between the two ideas and they are not mutually exclusive.

Interestingly, Velchick argued today that it would be a tall order for the outlets to claim irreparable harm for being blocked from the White House, because of the pool members who acted in solidarity by refusing to carry television feeds while their newsrooms were blocked from the White House.
“I would ask the court to try and analyze how, in practical terms, can they say that it is irreparable,” he said.

The administration has argued that it tried to ban CNN, Politico and MS Now from the White House on national security grounds. “They haven’t said they haven’t shown with any evidence that this was ban was implemented because of national security concerns,” Ted Boutrous said. “They haven’t shown that the ban that the reports jeopardize national security … They haven’t found that the ban helped them protect national security, and so the harm would be irreparable.”

Earlier, Boutrous argued that “one of the most important areas that journalists report on is national security, and it’s been going on in the White House and outside the White House since the beginning of our country”.
He added: “It’s extremely important for reporters to report on that andhold the government accountable.”
We’re following the key hearing in the Trump media ban case now, which is under way in DC district court.

Ted Boutrous, the lawyer representing CNN, MS Now and Politico, said today that Trump has “unambiguously said” that the grounds for barring these outlets is “because of what he perceives as negative, false, bad, not positive enough reporting”.

Boutrous noted that Steven Cheung, the White House communications director who he described as “no shrinking violet” also issued no declaration that there was a specific problem.

On the third day of his tour in Europe, Rubio expressed Washington’s mounting concern over the ability of the war in Ukraine to spread, more than four years after Russia invaded the country.

In an interview with Greece’s authoritative Kathimerini newspaper – published hours before he departed Athens for Portugal – Rubio said the conflict appeared to be mired in a “strategic stalemate which is a dangerous thing,” because a negotiated settlement was still far off.

body: Google is doing away with Safety Signal on Pixel Watch
Access to the emergency feature for LTE-connected wearables will end by December.

Here's an important heads up for any owners of some older Pixel Watches. Google will end support for its Safety Signal feature by the end of 2026. This tool was designed as a way to bring some core safety features to the smartwatch over LTE connectivity. It provided resources such as emergency SOS, fall detection and calls between emergency contacts even if the person didn't have a wireless plan for their wearable.
Safety Signal was only ever offered on the LTE-enabled Google Pixel Watch 2 and Google Pixel Watch 3 models, and now both versions of the smartwatch will be winding down support for the feature.

According to Google's own post, current Safety Signal users will receive email and push notifications with "advanced notice" about the coming change. The features will remain available during a 30-day transition period beginning from the date of the email. All access to Safety Signal will end by December 12.

The tools included under Safety Signal can still be used by those smartwatch models while on a WiFi network or while paired to a smartphone over Bluetooth. They can also be used if the watch is connected to a carrier's active cellular line.

articles.headline: Protesters blame 'vulture funds' for Spain's housing crisis
keyFacts: - Published Pierina Nicuray, a 21-year-old university graduate, has spent a week camped out in Madrid's Puerta del Sol square.
Like many of the hundreds of others who have pitched their tents here to protest at Spain's housing crisis, she has no doubts when it comes to diagnosing the cause.
"It's the same problem as always," she says.
body: - Published
Pierina Nicuray, a 21-year-old university graduate, has spent a week camped out in Madrid's Puerta del Sol square.
Like many of the hundreds of others who have pitched their tents here to protest at Spain's housing crisis, she has no doubts when it comes to diagnosing the cause.
"It's the same problem as always," she says. "A lack of homes."
She adds: "Landlords are taking advantage of the situation to raise rentals, and then there's also Airbnb."
Jorge Moreno, a 19-year-old film-dubbing student who has also been living in a tent here in central Madrid for the last few days, agrees.

"There are so many homes standing empty because they have been bought by vulture funds and investment funds which hike up the rent of people living in properties until they get rid of them," says Jorge, who lives with his mother and fears it will be a long time before he can afford a home of his own.
"They've been making a business of housing for a long time," he adds. "But it's an abusive business which stops Spaniards from being able to live in a decent home."
His and Pierina's diagnoses are frequently voiced by fellow protesters, ordinary Spaniards and even the Spanish government.

On presenting a recent package of emergency measures to tackle the housing problem, Socialist Prime Minister Pedro SÃ¡nchez said he was legislating "against those who consider housing just another object on the market with which to speculate".
Those reforms were rejected by Congress, prompting SÃ¡nchez to call a snap election next month.

Nicuray and Moreno can point to the single case that sparked the current Spanish housing protest movement as proof that profit-driven practices are at the heart of the crisis: the 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal was evicted from her home after the investment firm that had bought it tried to persuade her to leave, then sharply increased her rent, which she was unable to pay.
Although the social backlash that followed caused the company to invite Abascal to return to her old home, she never did, dying in hospital on Wednesday.
Many others have their own stories of struggling with a soaring rental market.
Carmen PÃ©rez is a retired widow, originally from Ecuador, who has been living in Spain for 17 years.

When she arrived, housing was relatively cheap and accessible, but - as costs have risen - she has been forced to move in with her daughter and son-in-law as she looks for somewhere affordable to rent.

"When a property is listed to rent, there's always a long waiting list," she says. "And the rent is always too high for me. All of this has affected my health - I've got depression, I don't have any stability or security."
Spain has seen an average rise in rental costs of 84% over the last 10 years, according to property outlet Idealista.
In the centre of the southern city of MÃ¡laga, the increase has been 113 %, and, in Marbella - just under 150%.
Such numbers have made housing Spaniards' biggest concern.

A recent study by the Centre for Sociological Research (CIS) showed how the broader Spanish population, like the protesters, want to see action taken against those perceived to be powerful movers in the housing market.
Some 72% wanted higher taxes introduced for those with 10 or more properties; 76% wanted limits on short-term tourist accommodation; and 40% supported the expropriation of empty homes.

However, Jorge Galindo, director at the Esade centre for economic policy, says that available data makes it difficult to know exactly how many Spanish properties are owned by so-called "vulture funds" and being used for speculation.
He points to Bank of Spain figures from 2024 showing that only 8% of properties for rent are owned by companies.
Galindo says he concludes from the data available that there is not a notable accumulation of property to rent among a small number of owners in Spain.
"When it comes to explaining the rise in rentals, that is not the big cause," he says. "What explains it is the shortage of supply compared to demand over recent years."
The Bank of Spain appears to agree, and has estimated that the country has a housing shortfall of around 750,000 homes.
The institution's deputy governor, Soledad NÃºÃ±ez, warned in September that by 2028 that could rise to one million.

There are 3.8 million empty properties in Spain, according to the National Statistics Institute (INE), but a large number of those are in depopulated rural areas and therefore have little relevance to the current crisis, which is most acute in urban hubs.
Other explanations for this high number include properties awaiting renovation, or legal disputes between family members who have inherited them.
Demographic changes play a major part in the imbalance between supply and demand.
Between 2021 and 2025, there were about 1.2 million new households in Spain, driven in great part by the arrival of migrants who have played a major role in the country's recent economic growth.
However, house building has not kept pace, with fewer than half-a-million new homes during that period.

That was partly because Spain's construction industry had shrunk in the wake of the Eurozone crisis, while the cost of materials rose substantially after Covid, and a lack of political consensus put legal obstacles in the way of building.
"It was not a priority for us to build new houses," Galindo says. "But, once the demographic boom came, we realised how costly it was for us."

He adds that short-term tourist accommodation, like Airbnb, which has been identified by both the Spanish government and many activists as a culprit, is likely to have had a more localised effect, pushing up prices in specific urban areas rather than having an overall impact.
Meanwhile, the crisis has been aggravated by lagging salaries.

A study by El PaÃs found that, in real terms, the average Spaniard had 5% less spending power than a decade ago, due to taxes, social security and inflation. The average monthly salary in the Madrid region is â¬1,550 (Â£1,314; $1,738).

"No worker should have to spend 75% or 80% of their salary on rent, because what are they supposed to eat?" says Francisco Pardo, an 81-year-old retired taxi driver, who sympathises with the protesters, during a visit to the tent city in Madrid.
"Many workers don't even earn â¬2,000 [per month]."
The case of Maricarmen has suddenly made the housing crisis an urgent topic of discussion, not just in Madrid's Puerta del Sol but across the country.
The question now is whether a consensus can be reached on how to solve it.

To be fair, Dave probably wants to turn it into a nice filet, so I don't blame it honestly.

In a statement, Mintrocket studio director Jaeho Hwang said, "Both games are set underwater, but Subnautica has such a distinct approach to underwater exploration, so working with the Subnautica 2 team gave us a chance to bring a new wave to Dave the Diver experience." Subnautica 2 creative director Anthony Gallegos shared some words on the collab too: "It’s clear that we both adore one another’s games a lot, and the expansion is a love letter to both Dave the Diver and the Subnautica universe. People are in for a treat."

No word if Dave will be making a counter appearance in Subnautica 2, though this doesn't feel particularly surprising given the fact that the latter is still in early access. keyFacts: President Trump on Thursday announced $2.4 billion in computing power commitments from major tech giants including Nvidia, OpenAI and Anthropic to support federal agencies’ AI-driven scientific research.

body: President Trump on Thursday announced $2.4 billion in computing power commitments from major tech giants including Nvidia, OpenAI and Anthropic to support federal agencies’ AI-driven scientific research.

The funding will be used to bring the Genesis Mission – an effort to use AI to improve federal scientific developments – to 14 agencies across energy, health and space, according to the Trump administration.
Nvidia is contributing $1 billion, the largest single donation. AMD has vowed to give $500 million, OpenAI is donating $200 million and Anthropic and Google have each pledged $150 million.

“With a $1 billion investment, Nvidia is putting advanced Super Intelligence in the hands of America’s scientists to accelerate breakthroughs in medicine, energy and materials,” Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said in a statement.
AMP and Emerald AI have committed $100 million each, while AWS, Armada, Crusoe and Micron are each chipping in $50 million, according to a press release.

The announcement was part of the White House’s “Science: A New Golden Age” summit on Thursday. The Trump administration initially launched the Genesis Mission in November 2025 through the Energy Department.
The pledges come as Trump has been pushing for broader acceptance of artificial intelligence or, as he calls it, “super intelligence.”

Leading tech executives – including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, OpenAI’s Sam Altman and SpaceXAI founder Elon Musk – have called for global cooperation to pace the development of the new tech after one researcher warned it could lead to human extinction.
The president has pushed back, arguing the greater threat is allowing China to win the AI race by slowing development of the latest, most powerful models at home.

Trump last week hosted the nation’s most powerful tech titans at an AI summit at the White House, welcoming execs from firms like Amazon, OpenAI and Google, who were collectively worth more than $1.8 trillion.

keyFacts: Johnny Silverhand is heading for the silver screen.
