body: Johnny Silverhand is heading for the silver screen. CD Projekt Red's sci-fi role-playing game Cyberpunk 2077 is being adapted into a live-action movie at Paramount Pictures, according to a new report, with the longtime producer of the Transformers series overseeing the project. It's the latest video game adaptation from Paramount, which is also bringing Street Fighter and Call of Duty to live-action.

According to Deadline, Transformers producer Lorenzo di Bonaventura is attached to produce the movie alongside CD Projekt Red. Di Bonaventura is also working on a new Transformers live-action movie with Steven Spielberg and Michael Bay.

Further details on the live-action Cyberpunk 2077 movie adaptation, including who will write, direct, and star in the film, weren't announced. But you know who'd be a good live-action Johnny Silverhand? Keanu Reeves. Just an idea!
Cyberpunk 2077 is ripe for adaptation

The futuristic sci-fi story of Cyberpunk 2077 is centered on the mercenary V, who accepts a job to steal a one-of-a-kind implant said to be the key to immortality. V is imbued with a cybernetic biochip that contains the memory and personality of legendary rock star (and terrorist) Johnny Silverhand, and the two are forced to work together to save V's life. The game's backdrop is the stylized and dystopian Night City, which is run by the powerful Arasaka Corporation.

Cyberpunk 2077 was released in 2020 — more than eight years after its original announcement — in an infamously dire state. In the following years, CD Projekt Red vastly improved upon the game, making it a fan favorite and delivering on the franchise's original cyberpunk vision. Cyberpunk 2077 has sold more than 40 million copies, according to Michał Nowakowski, joint-CEO of CD Projekt. The developer released an expansion, Cyberpunk 2077: Phantom Liberty, in 2025.

CD Projekt and Japanese animation studio Trigger have already adapted the world of Cyberpunk 2077 into an animated series, Cyberpunk: Edgerunners, which began streaming on Netflix in 2022. A stand-alone sequel series, Cyberpunk: Edgerunners 2, is slated to premiere on Netflix on Oct. 20.

A video game sequel to Cyberpunk 2077 was announced in 2022 under the working title Project Orion. In May 2025, CD Projekt announced that the sequel, now known as Cyberpunk 2, had entered pre-production. Cyberpunk 2 does not have an announced release date.

articles.headline: Ticket rises and more TV packages - why is price of sport increasing?
keyFacts: - Published At least Â£115 to watch a day of the Ashes in Birmingham - unless you are an Edgbaston member.
A minimum of Â£255 for a standard seat at the Wimbledon singles finals.
Prices starting from Â£289 for general admission to the British Grand Prix at Silverstone on raceday.
body: - Published
At least Â£115 to watch a day of the Ashes in Birmingham - unless you are an Edgbaston member.
A minimum of Â£255 for a standard seat at the Wimbledon singles finals.
Prices starting from Â£289 for general admission to the British Grand Prix at Silverstone on raceday.
Those are the ticket fees British sports fans have been told a single adult must pay if they want to attend some of the country's most beloved sports events in 2027.
The cost of entry to elite sport in the UK has risen sharply in the 2020s, but attendances across the majority of sports are as strong as ever.
Even for armchair fans watching at home, the breadth and expense of television subscriptions can be a barrier to accessing sport.
So what exactly is behind the rise in prices, can the increases possibly be justified and what does it all mean for fans?
In a new BBC Radio 5 Live programme - The Price of Our Sport - BBC Sport has taken a look.
What has happened to ticket costs?
Fans reacted with anger when some of the ticket price rises for major events next year were announced earlier this summer.

The increase in Ashes ticket prices is stark - the minimum price the last time Edgbaston held a Test in 2023 was Â£65, a rise of Â£50 to Â£115 in just four years. Admission to other venues, including The Oval, is even higher.
Last time out in Australia, some seats were sold to fans at all five venues for between Â£16 and Â£22.
At Wimbledon next year, the most expensive standard seat for both the men's and women's singles finals will be Â£400, Â£50 more than 2026, and more than double the cost from 2017.
That still makes Wimbledon the cheapest of the four Grand Slams, but even a Centre Court ticket for the middle Saturday of the tournament now costs at least Â£130.
General admission for Grand Prix Sunday at Silverstone is up to Â£289 from Â£189 in 2021, while the cheapest allocated seat now costs at least Â£609, up from Â£276 five years ago.
And general admission to the 2027 Ryder Cup at Adare Manor, in the Republic of Ireland, will cost â¬499 (Â£434), compared with up to â¬260 (Â£220) in Italy in 2023.
And other events which took place this year laid bare just how much more fans are being charged.
Fans paid Â£150 to attend a day of The Open at Royal Birkdale earlier this year, compared to Â£95 at St Andrews in 2022.
Prices for the FA Cup final varied from Â£50 to Â£285 in 2026, compared with Â£50 to Â£120 in 2016.
"It's just ludicrous," says Lee Hanlon, an England cricket fan who lives close to Edgbaston, but has decided not to attend next summer's Ashes because of the price rise.
"I'm angry. It seems like a lot of the normal cricket fans have been priced out. It seems like just people with money are going now.
"The increase is just too much. I find it upsetting."
But for event organisers, the prices chime with wider trends.

"We exist in an experience economy - we have definitely seen a subtle shift in the value people are placing on belonging, on the atmosphere you can be part of when you attend a live experience," says Mark Darbon, chief executive of the R&A, which operates golf's Open Championship.
"So when we set our prices we start by looking at some of the other major sporting events and benchmark ourselves, on price and value for money, by looking at what others are delivering."
How do organisers justify the ticket price rises?
In a poll on the BBC Sport website, 95% of respondents voted that tickets for the 2027 Ashes were too expensive.

A spokesperson for Edgbaston said: "Our entry-level ticket prices roughly match inflation compared to the last time Australia visited Edgbaston in 2023 - but like the rest of the country, we're battling increased costs and trying to manage these wherever we can."
Whether prices are set by governing bodies or the stadiums, the costs of putting on a major sports event include things like utilities, staffing, technology, insurance and marketing.
"Ticketing revenue generates less than 20% of our total revenue from The Open," Darbon says.

"We have seen really significant cost inflation in recent years. It now costs us 25% more than it did five or six years ago to host The Open - that could be Â£10-12m in incremental costs. We have to cover those costs."
Many prestige events and newly built venues also include an increased proportion of hospitality ticketing, which can drive up costs for fans wanting standard tickets.

"We are seeing more and more regular people willing to pay for a special experience at sport," says Richard Flint, chairman of Seat Unique, an online platform specialising in hospitality and VIP ticketing for events.
"Corporate boxes are being broken down more and more into individual seats, so it's less about people taking 10 of their colleagues and more about a couple, or four people, going together.
"[Teams and leagues] want to grow their revenue off the back of it, undeniably. Premium is much more open to people or go to one or two games a year, or who have travelled from abroad to come.
"Sometimes stadiums need updating and the revenue from premium ticketing can help fund a new stadium or new stand, so there are benefits to the everyday fan."
What about the cost to watch on TV?
In a world with increasingly volatile economics and changing consumer habits, broadcasting live sport has been one of the more reliable ways for companies to generate revenue.
And live sport - and entertainment - is one of the few industries whose financial success is unlikely to be significantly compromised by artificial intelligence in the coming years.

That means more and more companies have taken an interest in buying the rights to show sports events, which means more TV subscriptions than ever before are necessary for fans wanting to watch all of the action.

A football fan in the UK, for example, must subscribe to Sky Sports, TNT Sports, Amazon Prime and Premier Sports, if they want to watch all of the matches across the Premier League, Champions League and Scottish Premiership.
And they must pay for an annual TV licence to watch other matches on the BBC and ITV.
Without taking advantage of special offers, other sports can require even more subscriptions and even more money.

"It certainly helps when you can say to a fan that they only need to buy one subscription to see everything in one sport," says Pete Oliver, CEO of growth markets for DAZN, a global sports streaming service.
"If a sport is very fragmented, we would say it's not going to be a great proposition for the fan [for us to be involved], and it's probably not going to be a great commercial prospect for us.
"The cost of entertainment [subscriptions] generally will increase over time.

"There is natural inflation in the market, there is a lot of competition for sports rights, the athletes want to be paid more money, and the leagues want to do what is right for them, and if they can get somebody to pay more for the content, they will"

In some sports, including Premier League football, the money which leagues and clubs are earning from TV rights is by far their biggest source of income, but has plateaued to an extent in recent years.
So broadcasters are not necessarily always shelling out significantly higher costs for rights, but fans are still being charged more to watch.
Increased competition, growing operational costs and an uncertain long-term financial model all play a role.
"I think in the short term, the fans who are not going to illegal solutions are going to pay more to watch sport," says Pierre Maes, author and consultant in sports media rights.
"But we have reached a kind of roof - people have to pay a lot [and] we know that higher prices and more fragmentation leads to more piracy.
"People seem to have no moral obstacle to going with piracy. You can say that's bad, and that it's theft, but the reality is that people don't care.
"The music industry had to deal with this problem. In the long term, I think there is no other path than a Spotify of sports.
"Otherwise, sports will lose their fans and lose their attention."

articles.headline: Got a Microsoft 365 subscription? Your storage is about to shrink
keyFacts: ZDNET’s key takeaways - Microsoft 365 Family and Premium subscriptions are about to change.
- The new plans will offer shared pools of AI usage credits and OneDrive storage.
- Some subscribers could be forced to move data or pay double or triple their current rates.
body: ZDNET’s key takeaways
- Microsoft 365 Family and Premium subscriptions are about to change.
- The new plans will offer shared pools of AI usage credits and OneDrive storage.
- Some subscribers could be forced to move data or pay double or triple their current rates.

If you’ve been to the grocery store lately, you’re probably familiar with the phenomenon of shrinkflation — where the price of a bag of chips or a candy bar stays the same, but the product itself gets smaller.

Microsoft 365 subscribers are about to experience the cloud version of shrinkflation. Microsoft announced today that it will be making changes to its Microsoft 365 Personal, Family, Premium, and Pro subscriptions. The company is positioning the changes as giving subscribers “more flexibility with their AI and cloud storage benefits.” That may be true, but the net effect on subscribers who take full advantage of those subscriptions could be a huge price increase.
More from ZDNET
The changes, slated to roll out “in the coming months,” will affect shared AI usage and cloud storage benefits.
New storage and AI limits

The shrinkflation hits hardest at the shared OneDrive storage available through all these plans. Currently, if you have a Microsoft 365 Family, Premium, or Pro plan, each member has a fixed OneDrive storage allowance of 1 TB. If you’re the owner of one of those plans and you’ve used all five of your available shared slots, your family has a total of 6 TB of storage available.

After the changes take effect, these plans will get a shared storage pool for the entire subscription. Each family member’s accounts and files will remain private, but their usage will be subtracted from the shared pool. And the shrinkage is significant: Instead of 6 TB of storage divided evenly among six shared account holders, Microsoft 365 Family and Premium plans will get a total of 2 TB of shared storage.

Microsoft 365 Pro — a new plan that was very quietly launched in September — gets 5 TB of shared storage and the highest available AI usage limits, but that plan also comes with a hefty $100-a-month price tag.

For Microsoft 365 Family and Premium subscribers who are using more than 2 TB of total storage across all accounts and aren’t willing or able to cut their usage, the shrinkflation will turn into actual dollars-and-cents inflation. The base cost of a Microsoft 365 Family plan is $130 a year, or just a little over $10 per month. Each 1 TB of additional OneDrive storage adds $10 a month to the subscription price. So even if your family has used roughly half of your current total allowance, your bill could double or triple.

The change to AI benefits should be a little less painful. Currently, Copilot usage credits are available only to the subscription owner and can’t be shared with family members. After the changes take effect, family members will be able to share AI usage credits, and the subscription owner will be able to manage AI access for younger family members.
In addition, those plans will switch to a single AI usage allowance that can be shared by all family members. Premium and Pro subscribers will have the option to purchase additional AI usage credits.

According to a Microsoft spokesperson, new and upgraded subscriptions include shared storage starting Oct. 8, 2026. Customers with an existing subscription move to shared storage at their first renewal on or after May 2, 2027, and will be notified in advance.
Why is Microsoft doing this?

The most likely reason is to crack down on enthusiasts who are taking advantage of the 6 TB of storage included with a Family subscription to put together their own personal data hoard — just use a second free Microsoft account, give that account one of your shared subscription slots, and fill that OneDrive storage up. You can even use the sharing feature to make the storage from that secondary account available in your main account.

This isn’t the first time Microsoft has dramatically cut cloud storage allotments for OneDrive subscribers. In 2014, the company offered “unlimited” OneDrive storage to Office 365 subscribers. A year later, the company reneged on that promise. As I noted at the time:

Microsoft [blamed] a few greedy storage users for the change in heart. “A small number of users,” they wrote, “backed up numerous PCs and stored entire movie collections and DVR recordings. In some instances, this exceeded 75 TB per user or 14,000 times the average.”

Moving to shared storage and AI usage brings Microsoft’s plans into alignment with its main competitors. Google One, for example, includes 2 TB of shared storage for 6 people, plus AI credits, for $100 a year; a 5 TB plan costs $200 a year and includes additional AI credits. Apple sells shared storage via iCloud+ plans and with Apple One plans, which bundle Apple TV, Apple Music, and other subscription offerings.

For the majority of Microsoft 365 subscribers, this change will be unnoticeable. It’s likely that most Family plan subscriptions use less than the 2 TB allotment. But I suspect a significant percentage of subscribers use more than those new limits. That group includes many of Microsoft’s most loyal customers, the kind who’ve been encouraged for years to take advantage of the generous 1 TB per user allotments included with these plans. I expect to hear some very loud hollering from those customers.

articles.headline: Schumer, Jeffries dodge Mamdani controversy as fellow New York Dem unloads
keyFacts: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has come under fire for his comments on the Oct.
7, 2023, attack on Israel, but two leading voices in New York politics have so far remained quiet.

body: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has come under fire for his comments on the Oct. 7, 2023, attack on Israel, but two leading voices in New York politics have so far remained quiet.

Mamdani’s post on Wednesday briefly acknowledged Hamas’ blitz on Israel that left more than 1,100 Israelis dead and more than 250 others captured and held hostage by the terrorist organization. But the bulk of his statement spent time on criticizing Israel for its actions in Gaza in the three years since.

"The suffering did not begin nor end that day. It instead continued through the Israeli government’s devastating, ongoing genocide in Gaza, in which it has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians — including more than 21,000 children," Mamdani said on X. "Even since the so-called ceasefire, more than 1,400 Palestinians have been killed."
MAMDANI DOUBLES DOWN ON ANTI-ISRAEL OCT 7 STATEMENT AFTER BACKLASH

"That suffering has intensified with every Israeli bomb dropped on ambulances waiting outside hospitals, every drone strike targeting a residential building or journalist, and every shipment of food aid turned away at a border crossing," he continued. "Many New Yorkers are reckoning with this unbearable grief, and we mourn alongside them — all while knowing that our tax dollars fund these war crimes."
Mamdani notably did not mention the Jewish community in New York City, which is home to nearly 1 million Jews, according to a 2023 study from the UJA-Federation of New York.

And while at least one New York Democrat, Rep. Dan Goldman, laid into Mamdani for his comments, neither Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer nor House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, the two most powerful Democrats in Congress, has reacted.
MAMDANI’S $30M PLAN TO FIGHT ANTISEMITISM INCLUDES INCREASED FUNDING FOR ANTI-ISRAEL GROUP

"This is a reprehensible statement on the anniversary of the horrific terrorist attack by a Palestinian terrorist organization against innocent Israelis," Goldman said on X. "In the guise of ‘grieving’ with those mourning that day, Mayor Mamdani asserts as fact hotly disputed allegations that he knows full well will offend and further upset those same people he pretends to grieve with."
Neither Schumer nor Jeffries responded to requests for comment on Mamdani's remarks. They put out their own statements on the Oct. 7 attack on Wednesday.

Schumer, who is Jewish, noted that the attack was the "single deadliest day in Jewish history since the Holocaust." His support of Israel has become a wedge issue for some Senate Democrats, who have slowly pushed back against funding arms for Israel following three years of conflict in Gaza.
DEM SENATOR WHO DEMANDED SAUDI ACCOUNTABILITY OVER KHASHOGGI MEETS WITH CROWN PRINCE, PUSHES PALESTINIAN STATE

"Today, we reaffirm our commitment to the security of the Israeli people, to the aid and wellbeing of the Palestinian people and the recovery of the devastation in Gaza that the ensuing conflict brought, and to doubling down on efforts for a lasting peace resulting in two states where Israelis and Palestinians can live side by side in equal measures of peace, security, dignity, and mutual recognition," Schumer said.

Jeffries was more aligned with Schumer’s left flank in his statement, while recognizing that "we are reminded of the painful reality that the Jewish people are in a constant struggle for survival, as has been the case for thousands of years."

"Throughout the past three years, considerable suffering has plagued the Middle East. The horrific death of Palestinian civilians, destruction of civil society and devastation in Gaza is reprehensible and can never be allowed to happen again," Jeffries said.

"In order to end the vicious cycle of bloodshed, for the good of the Israeli and Palestinian people, American policy in the region must change dramatically," he continued. "We must commit to the creation of an independent Palestinian state to provide dignity, respect and self-determination for the Palestinian people."

articles.headline: New study shows concerning rise in developer burnout — and growing distrust in how AI may affect their jobs
keyFacts: While the overall response to the increasing use of AI is largely positive, growing concerns about the technology are clear, with little trust in the technology to make important decisions.

Stack Overflow’s annual survey is a useful look at how developers feel about the industry they work in, and highlights a growing friction between traditional software development and the growing role of AI tools.

The survey, by the Stack Overflow coding question-and-answer platform, also highlights a growth in solo employment, with 10.5% of respondents stating they freelance or are sole proprietors of a business, up from 3.9% in the previous years’ survey.
body: - A significant number of developers consider themselves to be suffering fatigue or burnout, study finds
- Devs are also concerned about the ethics of AI, and fear being replaced by automated coding tools
- The Stack Overflow Developer Survey compiled responses from 30,000 developers from 169 countries

A new industry survey exploring the state-of-developers has uncovered growing distrust in AI and concerns about fatigue and burnout. While the overall response to the increasing use of AI is largely positive, growing concerns about the technology are clear, with little trust in the technology to make important decisions.

Stack Overflow’s annual survey is a useful look at how developers feel about the industry they work in, and highlights a growing friction between traditional software development and the growing role of AI tools.

The survey, by the Stack Overflow coding question-and-answer platform, also highlights a growth in solo employment, with 10.5% of respondents stating they freelance or are sole proprietors of a business, up from 3.9% in the previous years’ survey.
Developer burnout

One key takeaway from the survey is that 45.1% of developers state they are “complacent” in their current roles, with around a third (32.6%) of respondents describing themselves as “unhappy” (just 22.3% are “happy.”) Of that 45.1% figure, burnout or fatigue were cited as the main cause (21.1%).

While remote work is still popular (34.8% of developers work wherever), the survey surfaces unclear, ambiguous priorities as a challenge, something that may inform general fatigue – or, indeed, feelings about AI.

Although many developers use AI (and search) to solve problems, its growing use within coding is being met with caution. Some 17.2% of developers don’t use AI tools, while assistants and agents are employed by 65.9%. But while developers are keen to learn new skills (52% have learned a new coding language in the past year), they are wary of AI’s consequences, with 17% concerned that it may replace them.
Critical skepticism
A read of the full survey paints a picture of an industry of skilled professionals finding their way in a new, unpredictable landscape – one that their own industry is responsible for.

Prashanth Chandrasekar, CEO of Stack Overflow says: “Developers are historically a highly skeptical group, and over the last year, as AI agents become rapidly more autonomous, that skepticism now acts as a critical safeguard.”

“As agents take on more work, developers need to know where an answer came from, what context informed the information that was produced or a decision that was made, and the most crucial piece — that they can actually verify its accuracy and relevance.

For those concerned about burnout and fatigue and their long-term careers, trust is perhaps the answer. “Trust is not a given when it comes to developers,” says Chandrasekar. “It is earned through transparency, source attribution, and rich technical context.”

articles.headline: High-severity Nvidia bug could crash GPU monitoring on exposed servers
keyFacts: Researchers found thousands of GPU servers exposing Nvidia's DCGM Exporter to the internet, with hundreds potentially vulnerable to a high-severity flaw that could let unauthenticated attackers crash the GPU monitoring service and disrupt AI workloads.
DCGM Exporters read telemetry from the GPUs on a host, including its hardware, utilization, memory usage, power consumption, and error events.
Each GPU has its own unique ID, or UUID, and all of these metrics are exposed in plaintext over HTTP.
body: Researchers found thousands of GPU servers exposing Nvidia's DCGM Exporter to the internet, with hundreds potentially vulnerable to a high-severity flaw that could let unauthenticated attackers crash the GPU monitoring service and disrupt AI workloads. DCGM Exporters read telemetry from the GPUs on a host, including its hardware, utilization, memory usage, power consumption, and error events. Each GPU has its own unique ID, or UUID, and all of these metrics are exposed in plaintext over HTTP. This exposure provides would-be attackers with detailed information useful for reconnaissance, including mapping GPU infrastructure, identifying potentially vulnerable systems, and monitoring workload activity. Michael Katchinskiy, a researcher at datacenter security startup Lava, found and reported the bug in the GPU health and performance monitoring service. In September, the GPU giant Nvidia released a fix for the flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-47483, and gave it an 8.2 CVSS high-severity rating. “Once we realized how much these endpoints revealed, the next question was: How many of them are exposed to the internet?” Katchinskiy said in a Thursday blog. So the researchers started scanning the internet for exposed DCGM Exporters. And the scale of exposure proved “especially significant,” he wrote. Over the course of four scans between March and May, the threat hunters found about 2,100 GPU servers exposing DCGM Exporter metrics to the open internet. These included 12,000 GPU UUIDs. None of these required authentication. The hosts belonged to about 300 organizations, according to Katchinskiy, and nearly half - 5,274 of the exposed GPUs, or 44 percent of the total - were located in the US. These GPUs represented about $100 million in hardware, and included Nvidia Blackwell Ultra B300 GPUs, H200s, and H100s - used to run large-scale AI workloads - plus consumer RTX 5090 and 4090 systems. While investigating the exposed systems, the Lava team found that about 25 percent of the exposed DCGM hosts also revealed data from Go’s /debug/pprof/ built-in profiling tool. The profiler collects and exposes runtime performance data such as CPU and memory usage for running Go applications. This includes CPU usage, memory allocations, goroutine states, and blocking events. “With enough concurrent unauthenticated requests, the exporter could run out of memory and crash, cutting off visibility into GPU health and activity,” Katchinskiy wrote. The CPU and memory pressure could also affect AI training or inference workloads. Nvidia fixed the issue in version 4.8.2, and operators should upgrade to that version or later. In addition to GPU telemetry, Lava looked into Prometheus Node Exporter, which monitors server hardware and operating systems, and also exposes metrics over HTTP. The team found 12,096 public Node Exporter hosts exposing data on server models, operating systems, firmware versions, hostnames, storage paths and networking hardware commonly used in GPU clusters. This information reveals how environments are built and configured, which could also be used by attackers for reconnaissance, matching the system to known vulnerabilities. The publicly exposed monitoring services affected customer infrastructure across neocloud and GPU cloud providers including Nebius, Voltage Park, Lambda, Northern Data, and DigitalOcean. Lava reported all of this to the affected providers, and Katchinskiy says that these providers worked with customers to address the exposures. For operators: the security shop says Nvidia DCGM Exporter, Node Exporter and Prometheus services should not be directly reachable from the public internet and recommends restricting them to authorized monitoring infrastructure. “The findings highlight a growing security gap in AI infrastructure: companies are spending millions on GPUs while leaving critical systems exposed,” Katchinskiy wrote. “Those exposures can reveal how AI environments are built and, in some cases, allow attackers to disrupt them.” ®

keyFacts: Enzo Maresca insists he’s calm about Manchester City being found guilty of all serious Premier League financial breaches.

body: Enzo Maresca insists he’s calm about Manchester City being found guilty of all serious Premier League financial breaches.

An independent commission over the international break deemed the multiple Premier League champions to have inflated sponsorships by around £900million from ‘sham’ companies, but Maresca supports the club.
Manchester City sit top of the Premier League but the future is uncertain Getty
The club deny all claims against them and have lodged an appeal , with that process now underway.
And in his first words since the verdict, the Italian threw all of his support behind the club and also insisted that his players aren’t distracted.
Speaking to the Manchester City official club channel, he said: “I am very calm. The club has been quite clear. We trust completely the club.
“We understand the noise, but the focus for us is just what we can control, and we can control the football side.
“The feeling is fantastic, to be honest.
“The players are excited and are just focused on that.
“They are not worried at all on different things. The noise is there, but they don’t care too much about the noise.”
Haaland calm despite charges verdict
This echoes what Erling Haaland had said in an interview with Sky Sports ahead of taking on Liverpool on Sunday in which he called for unity.
He said: “I think they [the fans] are going to have a good time.

“We have to stick together, we have to stay with each other and stay positive and no matter what happens in life, we always have to have a smile, so we have to stay positive, look ahead and try to win football games and try to enjoy the situation and the game.
Haaland didn’t directly mention the verdict, but he had a message of positivity for Man City fans Getty
“As I said, we have to stick together and we have to spread the love to eachother. Stick together and enjoy the ride and smile.”
Guardiola’s support
Former Man City manager Pep Guardiola has also thrown his support behind the club.
The Spaniard is expected to be at the Etihad Stadium next Wednesday for the Champions League game against Paris Saint-Germain, live on talkSPORT.
He also took to social media to express his support for the club.
He said: “I want every single Manchester City fan across the world to know I am here; more than ever.
“I am, always have been, always will be, behind my club, my owner, my chairman, Ferran (Soriano), the players, staff, Enzo (Maresca) and you, our unique supporters.
“Let me be clear: we will get through this together. I love you all.”
Guardiola was at Man City for two of the years in which they stand accused of cheating AFP
Maresca is likely to face difficult questions at the pre-match press conference AFP
Manchester City’s situation
During the international break, a 40 page statement from the independent commission posted on the Premier League website confirmed that Man City were guilty.
The key finding was that from 2009-2018, the club paid themselves through fake contracts to avoid Financial Fair Play and boost revenue.
That revenue was then used to buy players and build a team that won multiple trophies.
Man City submitted an appeal and that process is now underway, with their argument that the money they received came from the UAE government and not Sheikh Mansour .
One problem they may face is that Etihad, a key sponsor, have already denied that any funding they receive is from the government in a court battle in the United States.
But until the appeal process is complete, everything remains exactly the same.
There are also other forces at play with reports suggesting the UAE are going to pull money out of future investments in the UK depending on what happens to City.
Should they be found guilty and the appeal fails, there are a wide range of punishments .
These start with fines and transfer bans and go up to expulsion, points deductions and titles being stripped.
In the meantime, Man City will continue to play their fixtures as normal, starting with Liverpool on Sunday .

body: A Kentucky State University women’s basketball player from Senegal who was arrested by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has been released after spending two months in custody.
At a hearing on Tuesday, a judge granted Aminata Seck a $2,500 bond, which was posted on Wednesday after ICE did not appeal, according to Hishem Alsalman, managing attorney at Alsalman Law Office.
The judge found that Seck was neither a danger to the community nor a flight risk, Alsalman said on Thursday.
The judge also ruled that she could continue working towards her degree and praised her academic and athletic achievements.
Seck, 26, was detained on 7 August at Louisville Muhammad Ali International Airport as she was preparing to travel with her team to a tournament.

The Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, previously said in a statement that Seck had legally entered the United States in 2019 but then “chose to overstay her welcome in violation of our nation’s laws”. The agency said an immigration judge had ordered Seck’s removal a year earlier after she failed to appear at an immigration hearing.
Alsalman previously said an immigration judge had found that Seck did not receive notice of the earlier proceedings.
Seck is from Dakar, Senegal’s capital.

She was named to the Southern Intercollegiate Athletic Conference (SIAC) all-conference third team last season after leading her team with 11.7 points and 7.3 rebounds per game. The 6ft 4in center recorded five double-doubles and scored a season-high 30 points against Lane College on 14 January.

Seck was also named the winner of the SIAC Women’s Basketball Elite 16 award, the conference’s highest academic honor, presented to student-athletes who demonstrate exemplary performance in sport and the classroom.

body: Long before a wave of water rushed down the Bhote Koshi river and its tributaries, researchers were working to calculate just how many people are living downstream and exposed to potentially catastrophic flood risk in the areas that drain from Nepal’s high mountain basins.

The number they came up with — about 294,000 and growing — shows just how many people are living in areas of extreme risk in a country where climate change is destabilizing the rock and ice holding Himalayan slopes together and where meltwater is pooling in an ever-growing catalog of glacial lakes.

“For Nepal, it shows that there’s a lot of development going on very close to the river channel in these potentially hazardous zones,” said Scott Watson, a senior research fellow at the University of Leeds in England who studies glacial lakes. “That’s driven by tourism and the trade routes. The recent disaster was on the main trade route between Nepal and the Tibetan Plateau.”

The August disaster — when a massive rock and ice avalanche plunged off an almost 24,000-foot peak called Langtang Lirung and caused a debris flow that traveled about 120 miles — killed at least 1,455 people, and at least 5,285 people are still missing, according to Nepali authorities. Nearly 14,000 people were rescued.
If nothing is done, researchers say the number of people exposed will only grow.

“Hopefully, for Nepal, it’s kind of a bit of a wake-up call, this unfortunate recent disaster, in that there needs to be obviously a lot more focus on thinking about early warning systems, but also land use zoning,” Watson said. “We show that there’s a lot of buildings, there’s a lot of people very close to the river channel that are exposed to these hazards.”

About 108,000 of those people are downstream of glacial lakes, the researchers found. Many of those glacial lakes are pools of water dammed by ice that could fail and release a flush of water all at once.

The researchers started putting together this analysis in fall 2025, but it spent months undergoing academic peer review. They published their findings for the first time in the journal Scientific Reports on Thursday. The research is best viewed as a rough draft of where flood risk exists near Nepal’s high peaks — more thorough analysis is still needed.

The researchers performed their analysis by building a map of all rivers that originate in the transboundary areas of Nepal along the border with Tibet and India. They isolated areas within 50 kilometers, or 31 miles, downstream of glacial lakes or the headwaters of a river basin. Then, they mapped what would be exposed to floodwaters in a flood with 50 meters, or 164 vertical feet, of rising water downstream.
The researchers found about 108,000 people downstream of glacial lakes with ice that could fail and send a pulse of floodwater racing downstream.

Floods that rise 164 vertical feet and travel 31 miles might sound like an extraordinary occurrence. However, the August flooding in the Bhote Koshi river and its tributaries traveled about 120 miles downstream and raised water levels by roughly 330 feet in some communities, said Dipesh Chapagain, a senior scientist at the United Nations University Institute for Environment and Human Security.
“The risk could even be higher” than the paper suggests, said Chapagain, a Nepali scientist who studies climate change and flooding. “This event set a new level, a new threshold.”

Unlike the U.S., detailed flood hazard mapping is not available for much of Nepal. Watson said previous efforts to understand what portion of Nepal’s population is exposed to dangerous flooding that originates in the high mountains simply drew 1-kilometer (0.62-mile) buffers around alpine rivers.
Watson said the new research will inform where flood hazard mapping should be prioritized.

“We’re collecting very high-resolution elevation models to run some of the detailed flood hazard maps so we can focus on the most exposed hot spots,” Watson said. “To get into that level of detail, we kind of had to have this screening tool to say, you know, where are the hot spots?”

After more than a month of searching for missing people in the Bhote Koshi flooding, Nepal called off its search. The focus now, Chapagain said, is to build temporary settlements for thousands of flood victims. There is not a concrete plan yet for how to approach permanent resettlement, but Chapagain said new construction must be prioritized in safe areas.

“Future planning should consider all these risks when planning for new infrastructure projects, new settlements and also for the flood recovery projects,” Chapagain said, adding that flood early-warning systems should be prioritized in areas this study identified as high-risk.

Watson said the study shows that too much construction and development in Nepal has not been regulated. Hydropower investment and tourism are booming in Nepal, which has brought paved roads into high mountain catchments. The study found that the amount of area built within 50 vertical meters of riverbanks increased by approximately 46% from 2016 to 2023.

“Once those communities start to form, the amenities soon follow, your schools, your healthcare — you can quite quickly end up with a growing community in an area that’s actually very close to the river channel,” Watson said.

Meanwhile, he said thousands of glacial lakes are forming upstream as glaciers disappear and permafrost thaws due to climate change — and many could send a pulse of floodwater downstream with little notice or warning.

body: South Korea to recall its ambassador to Ukraine over North Korean POW dispute

SEOUL, South Korea — South Korea said Thursday it will recall its ambassador to Ukraine, stepping up its protest against Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's recent revelation of a supposedly secret transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea.
The South Korean announcement came days after its President Lee Jae Myung threatened to take unspecified punitive steps if Ukraine refuses to apologize over the revelation.

South Korea's Foreign Ministry didn't say when the ambassador, Park Hee-chang, will be brought back home. A ministry statement said that South Korea will continue consultations with Ukraine, adding it hopes the dispute between the two countries would be resolved smoothly.

South Korea and Ukraine became embroiled in a diplomatic row after Zelenskyy spoke about the transfer of the North Korean soldiers during his U.N. speech on Sept. 23. South Korea has accused Ukraine of violating a nondisclosure agreement on their transfer in mid-September, but Kyiv has denied agreeing to such a deal.

The soldiers were among thousands of North Korean troops deployed to support Russia's war against Ukraine. Since their capture in early 2025, the soldiers had expressed their desires to resettle in South Korea, because they could face persecution if repatriated home. South Korea had said it would accept them, because it legally regards the North as part of its territory and has a policy of accepting and financially supporting North Korean defectors.

South Korean officials said the non-disclosure agreement was made because they were concerned about the safety of the North Korean soldiers and their relatives in the North. But many experts say South Korea's liberal government likely also worries the disclosure of their arrival may hurt its efforts to improve ties with North Korea.

North Korea's state media hasn't commented on the soldiers' transfer. But the North previously reacted with fury to major defections of its citizens, accusing South Korea of kidnapping them. North Korea has shunned any talks with South Korea and the U.S. and focused on bolstering its nuclear program since 2019.

It's unclear what other steps South Korea would take. Experts say maintaining good relations with Ukraine is in South Korean national interests because Kyiv could provide Seoul with intelligence about North Korea's expanding cooperation with Russia and its battlefield experiences. They say cooperation with Ukraine is important for South Korea's partnerships with many Western countries supporting Ukraine over the war.
Observers say Zelenskyy disclosed the transfer of the North Korean POWs to expose the danger of North Korea's military support to Russia as a way to win more international assistance.
South Korea has provided $445 million in humanitarian assistance to Ukraine since 2022. In July, Lee pledged $100 million in aid to Ukraine in a meeting with Zelenskyy,
